extracted.intended_audience: machine learning researchers and practitioners working on federated learning, privacy engineers, and systems researchers
extracted.subtask_description: A broad survey of challenges, open problems, and technical desiderata for designing, analyzing, and deploying federated learning systems, with emphasis on optimization, communication, privacy, and systems integration. Targets researchers and practitioners seeking concrete research directions and system-level requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: When is a Global FL-trained Model Better?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine under what conditions the shared global model is better than independent per-device models; can we guarantee that the model h_FL learned via federated learning is at least as accurate as h_k when used for client k? Can we quantify how much improvement can be expected via federated learning? And can we develop personalization strategies with theoretical guarantees that at least match the performance of both natural baselines (h_k and h_FL)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This depends on data distribution across parties (e.g., vertical partitioning requires record linkage), robustness/privacy methods can make local models stronger for non-typical clients, and loss-factorization tricks can alleviate vertical partition assumptions; relates to multiple-source adaptation and agnostic federated learning. Practical and theoretical guarantees are open problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperparameter Tuning for FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperparameter optimization is challenging in FL: running many rounds with different hyperparameters on resource-constrained devices may be restrictive and expensive; FL adds hyperparameters (aggregation/global update rule, local client optimizer, clients per round, local steps per round, compression config, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research should develop efficient HPO for FL, easy-to-tune optimization algorithms, and adaptive or self-tuning algorithms robust across datasets and architectures. Goals include reducing communication/compute cost of HPO and producing optimizers whose same settings work across many real-world cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neural Architecture Design / NAS for FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Predefined deep learning architectures may be suboptimal for user-generated, potentially invisible and non-IID data; NAS could find architectures that are computationally efficient and better suited for FL data distributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider transferring gradient-based, evolutionary, or RL NAS methods to the federated setting; explore Weight Agnostic Neural Networks; study NAS for global or personalized models. Early exploration exists but distributing NAS over devices and communication-constrained settings is an open area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debugging and Interpretability under Privacy Constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced modelers inspect data subsets for sanity checking, debugging misclassifications, outliers, manual labeling, and bias detection—actions made difficult by decentralized data and privacy constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop privacy-preserving techniques (e.g., DP generative models trained with FL) to support debugging and interpretability tasks; many open questions remain regarding fidelity of DP generative models and other methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compression Objectives in FL
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several complementary practical compression objectives motivated by limited compute, memory and communication on devices: (a) gradient compression — reduce size of object communicated from clients to server; (b) model broadcast compression — reduce size of model broadcast from server to clients; (c) local computation reduction — make local training more computationally efficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (a) often has the largest practical impact due to slower uploads and averaging enabling aggressive lossy compression; (b) impact on convergence has only recently been studied; (c) can be realized jointly with (a) and (b). Methods addressing all three jointly are rare but valuable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility of Compression with Differential Privacy and Secure Aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many FL algorithms (Secure Aggregation, DP mechanisms) are not designed to work with compressed/quantized communications; naive application may break privacy or render compression ineffective (e.g., Secure Aggregation can add O(log M) bits per scalar, and DP noise mechanisms assume real-valued Gaussian/Laplacian noise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joint design of compression methods compatible with Secure Aggregation or for which DP guarantees can be obtained is an important open problem; consider biased estimators, discrete noise, and approaches that preserve DP/aggregation properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wireless-FL Co-design
rubrics_metrics.description: Wireless channel dynamics (interference, noisy channels, fluctuations) can undermine training latency and reliability in federated learning and should be accounted for in system design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential solutions include federated distillation (exchange logits), optimized worker scheduling, and leveraging wireless channel properties (broadcast/superposition) for analog aggregation to speed aggregation and training. Co-design of wireless and FL systems is necessary for mission-critical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instance-specific and Data-dependent Compression Guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: For gradient compression, current theoretical work often characterizes minimax worst-case behavior; in information theory compression guarantees are instance-specific (depend on entropy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop instance-specific guarantees for gradient compression and evaluate data-dependent compression schemes in the federated setting; learning compression schemes that adapt to data can yield better ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-device vs Cross-silo State Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: In cross-device FL, algorithms generally cannot assume any state is preserved on clients between rounds, whereas cross-silo FL (same clients participate repeatedly) can preserve state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects applicable techniques (error-correction, stateful protocols); cross-silo settings permit ideas like error-correction and protocols that rely on repeated participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact Final Model and Jointly Addressing Compression Objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional objective is to modify training such that the final model is compact and efficient for inference while also addressing gradient/model broadcast compression and local computation reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many compact-model techniques from ML exist but may not map straightforwardly to FL or may complicate training; research should target methods that yield compact final models without harming FL constraints and convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extending FL to Other ML Paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: Federated learning has primarily focused on supervised learning; extending FL to reinforcement learning, semi-supervised and unsupervised learning, active learning, and online learning presents open challenges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore paradigm-specific challenges (labels availability, temporal aspects, exploration/exploitation, streaming data) and design FL algorithms that accommodate these learning setups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporating Bayesian Methods for Uncertainty and Robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Bayesian neural networks and probabilistic approaches provide uncertainty estimates, robustness to overfitting, and help reason about confidence—potential conceptual improvement for FL, especially with small datasets and non-IID aggregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preliminary work shows promise for aggregation across non-IID data, but scalability and computational feasibility in FL need investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy Goal: Data Minimization and Limited Information Flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideal privacy properties: each actor learns nothing more than needed for their role (e.g., analyst only learns whether a metric exceeds a threshold), and raw user data never leaves the device—model updates are more focused and often ephemeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems to minimize information flow (early data minimization), ensure participants can reason about what personal information may be revealed, and measure privacy of the complete system against ideal goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy in Depth (Graceful Degradation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose modular units with layered protections so the system's privacy properties degrade gracefully if a technique fails, analogous to defense in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layer multiple strategies (e.g., MPC within a TEE) and prefer primitive flows (e.g., sending gradient updates to a server-side TEE rather than raw examples) so that privacy expectations deteriorate slowly if assumptions are violated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Threat Models and Actor-specific Guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: Precisely characterize actors (clients, server, analysts, deployed models, rest of world) and their threat capabilities (malicious vs honest-but-curious, root access), and provide guarantees tailored to these views (Table 7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and analyze guarantees that specify which actors are protected against which adversarial capabilities; consider TEEs reducing threat power; be explicit about assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify Assumptions and Privacy Parameters Explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Precisely specifying assumptions and privacy goals often implicates concrete parameters (ε, ε', ε0, γ, σ, etc.) and concepts like differential privacy and honest-but-curious security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State adversary strength and parameter values under which guarantees hold; analyze how guarantees degrade if adversary strength increases beyond assumed limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three Privacy Aspects to Address in FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Privacy design must address (1) how f is computed and intermediate information flow (secure computation), (2) what is computed and how much a result reveals (privacy-preserving disclosure, differential privacy), and (3) verifiability (prove faithful behavior without revealing private data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use MPC/TEEs for computation-flow protection, DP for limiting disclosure from outputs, and remote attestation or zero-knowledge proofs for verifiability. End-to-end composition of these aspects is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure Computation Technologies and Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Technologies such as Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC), Homomorphic Encryption (HE), and Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) have distinct properties: MPC enables collaborative computation revealing only outputs; HE permits operations on ciphertexts; TEEs provide confidentiality/integrity/attestation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider practical limitations: finite-field arithmetic complicates real numbers, quantization is needed, generic MPC can be impractical, HE raises key-management issues, and TEEs have trust/attestation constraints. Choose or design primitives with ML and FL constraints in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPC Practicality for ML in FL
rubrics_metrics.description: While any function can be securely computed, generic MPC solutions often have prohibitive performance; custom protocols for linear/logistic regression and neural network training/inference exist (typically in cross-silo settings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porting MPC protocols to cross-device FL is challenging due to communication overhead; focus on custom, communication-efficient protocols or delegate to small non-colluding server groups where feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homomorphic Encryption Key and Trust Considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Using HE in FL raises questions about who holds secret keys and key renewal requirements; relying on a trusted non-colluding party is non-standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate deployment models for HE (who holds keys, how keys rotate) and feasibility given FL's trust assumptions; consider hybrid approaches or external key-management solutions cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differential Privacy Variants and Their Roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Different instantiations of differential privacy (local, central, shuffled, aggregated, hybrid) quantify how much information about an individual can be learned from outputs; algorithms with DP incorporate randomness/noise tuned to mask users' influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select DP model appropriate to threat model and system architecture; tune noise parameters to trade off privacy and utility; consider shuffled/aggregated models for better practical trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verifiability Techniques for FL
rubrics_metrics.description: Verifiability pertains to proving to others that parties executed desired behavior faithfully without revealing private data; techniques include remote attestation and zero-knowledge proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate attestation for TEEs and cryptographic proofs where clients or servers must demonstrate correct protocol execution, balancing overhead with assurance needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete Threat Descriptions per Data/Access Point
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients: malicious clients can inspect messages and tamper with training; honest-but-curious clients inspect but not tamper. Server: malicious server inspects and tampers; honest-but-curious inspects only. Analysts: may access multiple outputs. Deployed models: compromised devices may have black-box or white-box access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this threat breakdown to determine which protections (MPC, DP, TEEs, access control) are necessary at each point; design defenses accordingly and be explicit about which actor views are protected.
